user_context.prompt: I need a 45-minute crash course on eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and spectral decomposition so I can understand how Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces dimensionality in machine learning.
user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, symmetric matrix spectral theorem, and how covariance matrix eigenvectors define principal components in PCA.

candidate_course.title: Spectral Decomposition to PCA: Geometry and Algebra of Eigenvectors
candidate_course.description: A focused 45-minute course bridging linear transformations and eigen-analysis with symmetric covariance matrices and Principal Component Analysis.
candidate_course.target_audience: Intermediate learners with basic matrix multiplication knowledge aiming to understand PCA mathematically.

modules.title: Geometric Intuition and Characteristic Polynomials
modules.learning_objective: Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2x2 matrices and interpret them as invariant directions under linear transformations.
modules.summary: Covers the equation Av = lambda v, determinant condition det(A - lambda I) = 0, and finding eigenspaces.
sample_question_prompts: Find the eigenvalues of A = [[3, 1], [1, 3]] by solving det(A - lambda I) = 0.
Why must v be non-zero in the definition Av = lambda v, whereas lambda = 0 is valid?

modules.title: The Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices
modules.learning_objective: Explain why real symmetric matrices always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, enabling A = Q Lambda Q^T.
modules.summary: Introduces orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices and why sample covariance matrices Sigma = (1/n) X^T X are positive semi-definite.
sample_question_prompts: If A is a real symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues lambda_1 and lambda_2, prove that their eigenvectors v_1 and v_2 are orthogonal.
What does positive semi-definiteness of the covariance matrix imply about its eigenvalues?

modules.title: Variance Maximization and Principal Components
modules.learning_objective: Connect the top-k eigenvectors of the covariance matrix to the directions of maximum projected variance in PCA.
modules.summary: Formulates PCA via the Rayleigh quotient u^T Sigma u / (u^T u) and shows how projecting onto the top-k eigenvectors preserves maximum variance.
sample_question_prompts: Given eigenvalues [12.4, 3.1, 0.5] of a 3D covariance matrix, what fraction of total variance is retained by projecting onto the first two principal components?
Show using the spectral decomposition Sigma = Q Lambda Q^T why the unit vector maximizing u^T Sigma u is the eigenvector corresponding to lambda_max.

expected.rationale: The course directly addresses the learner's goal of connecting eigenvalues and spectral decomposition to PCA within a 3-module structure well-suited for 45 minutes. Each module balances conceptual multiple-choice checks with short-answer derivations.

user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: Correctness invariants, negative edge handling, time complexity, and residual graph augmenting path mechanics for shortest path and network flow algorithms.

candidate_course.title: Shortest Paths, Residual Networks, and Max-Flow Duality
candidate_course.description: Rigorous analysis of relaxation-based shortest path algorithms and augmenting-path network flow algorithms.
candidate_course.target_audience: Advanced computer science students preparing for graduate-level algorithm analysis.

modules.title: Edge Relaxation, Dijkstra's Greedy Invariant, and Negative Weights
modules.learning_objective: Prove when Dijkstra's greedy selection invariant holds and construct a counterexample with negative-weight edges.
modules.summary: Analyzes the triangle inequality relaxation property, priority queue complexity O((V + E) log V), and failure under negative edges.
sample_question_prompts: Construct a 3-vertex DAG with a negative edge weight where Dijkstra's algorithm without re-popping vertices fails.
What invariant holds for the settled set S at each step of Dijkstra's algorithm on non-negative graphs?

modules.title: Bellman-Ford Dynamic Programming and Negative Cycle Detection
modules.learning_objective: Derive the V-1 relaxation round bound of Bellman-Ford and explain how round V detects reachable negative-weight cycles.
modules.summary: Examines path-length induction over at most V-1 edges in simple paths and how negative cycle detection relates to arbitrage and feasibility.
sample_question_prompts: Why does any shortest simple path in a graph with V vertices and no negative cycles contain at most V - 1 edges?
Which edge relaxation condition after V - 1 iterations certifies a reachable negative-weight cycle?

modules.title: Residual Graphs, Ford-Fulkerson, and the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
modules.learning_objective: Trace augmenting paths in residual networks G_f and prove the equivalence of maximum flow value and minimum s-t cut capacity.
modules.summary: Defines forward and backward residual capacities, bottleneck augmentation, and the equivalence of: (1) f is a max flow, (2) G_f has no augmenting path, (3) |f| = c(S, T).
sample_question_prompts: Why are backward edges with capacity f(u, v) required in the residual network G_f?
Given a flow network where no s-t path exists in G_f, define the vertex set S that yields a cut (S, T) with capacity equal to |f|.

modules.title: Edmonds-Karp Shortest Augmenting Paths and Polynomial Complexity
modules.learning_objective: Explain how choosing shortest augmenting paths via BFS bounds augmentations to O(VE) and total runtime to O(VE^2).
modules.summary: Contrasts irrational/large-capacity pathological cases in generic Ford-Fulkerson with BFS distance monotonicity in Edmonds-Karp.
sample_question_prompts: How many times can a specific edge (u, v) become critical (saturated) along shortest augmenting paths in Edmonds-Karp, and why?
What is the worst-case time complexity of Ford-Fulkerson with integer capacities vs. Edmonds-Karp?

expected.rationale: This 4-module curriculum hits every graduate exam requirement: greedy vs DP shortest paths, residual backward edge necessity, Max-Flow Min-Cut proof structure, and Edmonds-Karp complexity bounds.

modules.learning_objective: Compute point addition and point doubling on y^2 = x^3 + ax + b (mod p) and verify abelian group properties.
modules.summary: Covers the non-singularity discriminant condition 4a^3 + 27b^2 != 0 (mod p), the point at infinity O as identity, and algebraic slope formulas.
sample_question_prompts: Why is the condition 4a^3 + 27b^2 != 0 (mod p) necessary for E(F_p) to form a valid group?
Given P = (x_1, y_1) on E(F_p), what is its additive inverse -P and why does P + (-P) = O?

modules.title: Scalar Multiplication and the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP)
modules.learning_objective: Analyze double-and-add scalar multiplication kG in O(log k) group operations and state the ECDLP hardness assumption.
modules.summary: Contrasts the O(log n) forward computation Q = xG with the O(sqrt(n)) Pollard's rho barrier for recovering scalar x from (G, Q) in prime-order subgroups.

modules.title: The Schnorr Identification Protocol: Completeness and Special Soundness
modules.learning_objective: Prove completeness of the 3-move Schnorr protocol (R = kG, challenge c, response s = k + cx mod q) and extract the witness x from two transcripts with the same commitment.
modules.summary: Walks through commitment R, verifier challenge c, response s, verification sG == R + cQ, and the special soundness extractor x = (s_1 - s_2)(c_1 - c_2)^(-1) mod q.
sample_question_prompts: If a prover reuses the same nonce k for two distinct challenges c_1 != c_2, derive the algebraic formula that recovers the secret key x.

modules.title: Honest-Verifier Zero-Knowledge Simulation and the Fiat-Shamir Transform
modules.learning_objective: Construct the HVZK simulator for Schnorr transcripts and explain how hashing the commitment and statement (c = H(G, Q, R, m)) produces a non-interactive proof.
modules.summary: Demonstrates how a simulator samples (c, s) uniformly at random and computes R = sG - cQ without knowing x, and explains why omitting Q or R from the Fiat-Shamir hash breaks soundness.
sample_question_prompts: Explain why the simulated transcript (R = sG - cQ, c, s) has the exact same probability distribution as an honest prover's transcript.
What forgery attack becomes possible in Fiat-Shamir Schnorr if the commitment R is omitted from the hash input c = H(m)?

expected.rationale: Accurately progresses from the elliptic curve group law over F_p to scalar multiplication/ECDLP and then to Schnorr's completeness, special soundness witness extraction, HVZK simulation, and Fiat-Shamir.

modules.title: Stochastic Transition Matrices and Stationary Distributions
modules.learning_objective: Formulate the Markov property, compute multi-step transitions P^t, and solve pi P = pi for a stationary distribution.
modules.summary: Introduces row-stochastic matrices, state distribution evolution, and solving the left eigenvector equation pi P = pi with sum(pi_i) = 1.
sample_question_prompts: Given transition matrix P = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]], solve pi P = pi subject to pi_1 + pi_2 = 1.

modules.title: Ergodicity: Irreducibility, Aperiodicity, and Detailed Balance
modules.learning_objective: Distinguish between existence of a stationary distribution and convergence to it, and verify stationarity via the detailed balance condition pi_i P_ij = pi_j P_ji.
modules.summary: Explains periodic vs reducible chains and proves that if pi_i P_ij = pi_j P_ji holds for all i, j, then pi is stationary.
sample_question_prompts: Give an example of a 2-state irreducible Markov chain that has a unique stationary distribution pi but fails to converge to pi from arbitrary initial states.
Prove in two lines that summing the detailed balance equation pi_i P_ij = pi_j P_ji over all i yields (pi P)_j = pi_j.

modules.title: Metropolis-Hastings and Cancellation of the Normalization Constant
modules.learning_objective: Derive the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability alpha(x, x') and explain why the intractable Bayesian evidence Z cancels out.
modules.summary: Shows how proposing x' ~ q(x'|x) and accepting with alpha(x, x') = min(1, [p~(x') q(x|x')] / [p~(x) q(x'|x)]) enforces detailed balance with respect to the posterior p(x) = p~(x)/Z.
sample_question_prompts: Why does the marginal likelihood Z = integral p(D|theta)p(theta) d_theta disappear in the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio?
How does the acceptance ratio simplify when the proposal distribution is symmetric, q(x'|x) = q(x|x')?

expected.rationale: Tightly structured 3-module progression from transition matrices to ergodicity/detailed balance and finally the Metropolis-Hastings ratio, directly answering how unnormalized Bayesian posteriors are sampled.

module_context.module_title: Geometric Intuition and Characteristic Polynomials
module_context.learning_objective: Compute eigenvalues of 2x2 matrices and verify them using trace and determinant invariants.

candidate_question.prompt: Consider the symmetric matrix A = [[4, 2], [2, 1]]. What are the eigenvalues of A, and which invariant pair confirms your answer?
options: lambda_1 = 5, lambda_2 = 0, verified because lambda_1 + lambda_2 = tr(A) = 5 and lambda_1 * lambda_2 = det(A) = 4(1) - 2(2) = 0
lambda_1 = 4, lambda_2 = 1, verified because the eigenvalues of any symmetric matrix equal its diagonal entries
lambda_1 = 3, lambda_2 = 2, verified because lambda_1 + lambda_2 = tr(A) = 5 and det(A) = 4(1) + 2(2) = 8
lambda_1 = -5, lambda_2 = 0, verified because det(A - lambda I) = lambda^2 + 5*lambda = 0
candidate_question.correct_answer: lambda_1 = 5, lambda_2 = 0, verified because lambda_1 + lambda_2 = tr(A) = 5 and lambda_1 * lambda_2 = det(A) = 4(1) - 2(2) = 0
candidate_question.grading_notes: Option A is correct: det(A - lambda I) = (4 - lambda)(1 - lambda) - 4 = lambda^2 - 5*lambda = 0, giving roots 5 and 0. Option B tests the diagonal misconception; Option C tests the determinant sign error; Option D tests the trace sign error in lambda^2 - tr(A)lambda + det(A) = 0.

expected.rationale: The question directly targets the student's prior sign error in expanding det(A - lambda I) and reinforces the trace/determinant invariant check, with each distractor diagnostic of a specific algebraic misconception.

module_context.course_title: Shortest Paths, Residual Networks, and Max-Flow Duality
module_context.module_title: Edge Relaxation, Dijkstra's Greedy Invariant, and Negative Weights
module_context.learning_objective: Prove when Dijkstra's greedy selection invariant holds and construct a counterexample with negative-weight edges.

candidate_question.prompt: Consider a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with vertices {S, A, B} and directed edges: S -> A (weight 2), S -> B (weight 5), and B -> A (weight -4). If standard Dijkstra's algorithm (which never re-processes a vertex once popped from the priority queue) is run from source S, what happens?
options: It pops S (d=0), then pops A (d=2) and permanently locks d[A]=2, failing to update A to the true shortest path S -> B -> A of total weight 5 + (-4) = 1 (or even if it updates d[A]=1 when relaxing B -> A, A was already settled and any outgoing edges from A would have been relaxed with the wrong distance).
It enters an infinite loop between B and A because any negative edge weight creates a negative cycle.
It computes the correct shortest path distances for all vertices because the graph is a DAG and has no negative cycles.
It pops B before A because 5 > 2, and therefore finds the path of weight 1 first.
candidate_question.correct_answer: It pops S (d=0), then pops A (d=2) and permanently locks d[A]=2, failing to update A to the true shortest path S -> B -> A of total weight 5 + (-4) = 1 (or even if it updates d[A]=1 when relaxing B -> A, A was already settled and any outgoing edges from A would have been relaxed with the wrong distance).
candidate_question.grading_notes: Directly refutes the misconception that Dijkstra only fails on negative cycles by showing a concrete 3-node DAG where settling A at d=2 violates the greedy monotone path extension assumption.

expected.rationale: Presents a crisp 3-vertex DAG counterexample that directly targets the learner's prior misconception that negative cycles are required for Dijkstra to fail.

user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: Using Tarjan's potential method to prove O(1) amortized insertion in a dynamic array that doubles capacity when full.
user_context.prior_feedback_summary: Learner understood the aggregate method sum of powers of 2, and now wants to practice writing a formal potential function proof.

module_context.module_title: Tarjan's Potential Method
module_context.learning_objective: Define a potential function Phi(D_i) >= 0 and bound amortized cost c_hat_i = c_i + Phi(D_i) - Phi(D_{i-1}).

candidate_question.prompt: A dynamic array has current size n_i and capacity m_i (initialized with n_0 = 0, m_0 = 1). When n_{i-1} < m_{i-1}, inserting an element costs c_i = 1. When n_{i-1} = m_{i-1}, the array allocates a new buffer of capacity m_i = 2 * m_{i-1}, copies all n_{i-1} elements, and inserts the new element, costing c_i = n_{i-1} + 1 = n_i. Using the potential function Phi_i = 2*n_i - m_i, show that Phi_i >= 0 for all i >= 1 and compute the amortized cost c_hat_i = c_i + Phi_i - Phi_{i-1} in both the non-resizing and resizing cases.
candidate_question.correct_answer: Since the array doubles whenever full, for all i >= 1 we have n_i >= m_i / 2, so Phi_i = 2*n_i - m_i >= 0. Case 1 (no resize, n_i = n_{i-1} + 1, m_i = m_{i-1}): c_hat_i = 1 + (2*n_i - m_i) - (2*(n_i - 1) - m_i) = 1 + 2 = 3. Case 2 (resize, n_{i-1} = m_{i-1}, m_i = 2*n_{i-1}, n_i = n_{i-1} + 1): actual cost c_i = n_{i-1} + 1. Change in potential: Phi_i - Phi_{i-1} = (2*(n_{i-1} + 1) - 2*n_{i-1}) - (2*n_{i-1} - n_{i-1}) = 2 - n_{i-1}. Thus c_hat_i = (n_{i-1} + 1) + (2 - n_{i-1}) = 3 = O(1).
candidate_question.grading_notes: Award full credit if the student shows: (1) non-negativity via the load factor invariant n_i >= m_i / 2, (2) non-resizing amortized cost = 3, and (3) resizing amortized cost where the +n_{i-1} copy cost cancels against the -n_{i-1} drop in potential to give 3.

expected.rationale: Explicitly specifies the indexing, initial state, actual cost model c_i, and potential function Phi_i = 2n_i - m_i, allowing the advanced student to execute a clean, unambiguous derivation.

module_context.course_title: Elliptic Curve Groups, Discrete Logarithms, and Schnorr Zero-Knowledge Proofs
module_context.module_title: The Schnorr Identification Protocol: Completeness and Special Soundness
module_context.learning_objective: Extract the secret key x from two accepting Schnorr transcripts sharing the same commitment R.

candidate_question.prompt: In a prime-order group of order q with generator G and public key Q = xG, a prover produces two valid Schnorr transcripts (R, c_1, s_1) and (R, c_2, s_2) using the same nonce commitment R = kG for two distinct challenges c_1 != c_2 (mod q), where s_i = k + c_i * x (mod q). Derive the explicit formula for the secret witness x in terms of s_1, s_2, c_1, c_2 modulo q, and state why the prime order q guarantees that the modular inverse exists.
candidate_question.correct_answer: Subtracting the two response equations modulo q eliminates the unknown nonce k: s_1 - s_2 = (k + c_1*x) - (k + c_2*x) = (c_1 - c_2)*x (mod q). Since c_1 != c_2 (mod q) and q is prime, gcd(c_1 - c_2, q) = 1, so (c_1 - c_2) has a unique multiplicative inverse modulo q. Multiplying both sides by (c_1 - c_2)^(-1) mod q yields x = (s_1 - s_2) * (c_1 - c_2)^(-1) mod q.
candidate_question.grading_notes: Must include: (1) subtracting s_1 and s_2 to eliminate k, (2) solving x = (s_1 - s_2)(c_1 - c_2)^(-1) mod q, and (3) explaining that c_1 - c_2 != 0 mod q in field F_q (since q is prime) ensures invertibility.

expected.rationale: Well-scoped algebraic derivation that connects practical cryptographic catastrophic failure (nonce reuse) with formal ZK special soundness extraction and finite field invertibility.

question.prompt: Given n items with weights w[1..n] and values v[1..n] and knapsack capacity W, define the DP state dp[i][c], write its transition recurrence, and state the time and space complexity (including the 1D rolling-array space optimization).

Transition: dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c] if w[i] > c, else max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c - w[i]] + v[i]). Time complexity is O(nW) and space complexity is O(nW), which optimizes to O(W) by iterating c backwards from W down to w[i] in a 1D array.

question.grading_rubric: For practical interview prep, require clear state definition, correct include/exclude recurrence, and O(nW) time / O(W) reverse-loop space complexity. Formal inductive proof of optimal substructure is not required for this user profile.

This takes O(n * W) time and O(n * W) space, or O(W) space if we use a 1D array and loop c from W down to w[i] so we don't reuse item i multiple times.

module_context.course_title: Graduate Design and Analysis of Algorithms
module_context.module_title: Proving Optimal Substructure and DP Correctness by Induction
module_context.learning_objective: Prove by mathematical induction and exchange/cut-and-paste argument that the 0/1 Knapsack recurrence computes the globally optimal subset value.

prior_misconceptions: Stating a recurrence formula without proving the inductive hypothesis or optimal substructure via contradiction

question.prompt: Prove by induction on i that dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c - w_i] + v_i) correctly equals OPT(i, c), the maximum value of any valid subset S subseteq {1, ..., i} with weight at most c. Your answer must state the inductive hypothesis, justify optimal substructure via a cut-and-paste contradiction argument for the two cases (i in S* vs i not in S*), and state why O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial.
question.reference_answer: Inductive Hypothesis: For a fixed i-1, assume dp[i-1][c'] = OPT(i-1, c') for all 0 <= c' <= W. Base case i=0: only the empty set is valid, so dp[0][c] = 0 = OPT(0, c). Inductive step for i: Let S* be an optimal subset for (i, c). Case 1 (i not in S*): S* subseteq {1..i-1} with weight <= c, so OPT(i, c) = OPT(i-1, c) = dp[i-1][c] by IH. Case 2 (i in S*, possible only if w_i <= c): Then S' = S* \ {i} is a valid subset of {1..i-1} with weight <= c - w_i. If val(S') < OPT(i-1, c - w_i), we could cut S' and paste an optimal T* for (i-1, c - w_i) to get T* U {i} with strictly greater value than S*, contradicting optimality of S*. Thus OPT(i, c) = OPT(i-1, c - w_i) + v_i = dp[i-1][c - w_i] + v_i by IH. Taking the max over both cases proves dp[i][c] = OPT(i, c). Finally, O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial because W is exponential in its bit-length log_2(W).
required_concepts_for_user_goal: explicit inductive hypothesis dp[i-1][c'] = OPT(i-1, c') for all c' <= W
cut-and-paste contradiction proof that S* \ {i} must be optimal for subproblem (i-1, c - w_i)
pseudo-polynomial distinction: O(nW) is exponential in the input bit-length of W (log_2 W)
question.grading_rubric: Because rigor_preference is rigorous_formal and the user is preparing for graduate proof exams, merely writing the recurrence and O(nW) runtime without the inductive hypothesis, cut-and-paste contradiction argument, and pseudo-polynomial bit-length explanation is insufficient (is_right: false, partially_correct).

user_submission.answer: dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c - w_i] + v_i) because for item i you either leave it out or put it in the knapsack. Since there are n items and W capacities, the runtime is O(nW).

cut-and-paste contradiction proof that S* \ {i} must be optimal for subproblem (i-1, c - w_i)
pseudo-polynomial distinction: O(nW) is exponential in the input bit-length of W (log_2 W)

module_context.module_title: Recursion Trees and the Master Theorem
module_context.learning_objective: Compare n^(log_b a) against f(n) to determine asymptotic runtime of divide-and-conquer recurrences.

question.prompt: Using recursion-tree intuition or the Master Theorem, what is the tight asymptotic runtime Theta(...) of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n, and why does the n term not show up in the final Big-Theta bound?
question.reference_answer: Here a = 4, b = 2, so the number of leaves in the recursion tree grows as n^(log_2 4) = n^2, which polynomially dominates the root non-recursive work f(n) = n (Case 1 / leaf-heavy). Because the work per level quadruples every time the problem size halves (n, 2n, 4n, ..., n^2 at the leaves), the geometric series is dominated by the bottom level, giving T(n) = Theta(n^2).
required_concepts_for_user_goal: critical exponent n^(log_b a) = n^(log_2 4) = n^2
leaf-heavy / Case 1 dominance over f(n) = n yielding Theta(n^2)
question.grading_rubric: For conceptual_intuition interview prep, award full credit (`is_right: true`) if the learner computes n^(log_2 4) = n^2, identifies that leaf work dominates the linear work f(n) = n (geometric growth across levels), and concludes Theta(n^2).

user_submission.answer: At each level we branch into 4 subproblems of size n/2, so the leaf count is 4^(log_2 n) = n^(log_2 4) = n^2. Since n^2 is polynomially larger than the O(n) work per call (work doubles each level down the tree: n, 2n, 4n...), the leaves dominate the geometric sum and the total runtime is Theta(n^2).

matched_concepts: critical exponent n^(log_b a) = n^(log_2 4) = n^2
leaf-heavy / Case 1 dominance over f(n) = n yielding Theta(n^2)
expected_decision.feedback_focus: Validate their recursion-tree geometric series intuition (n + 2n + 4n + ... + n^2 = Theta(n^2)).
expected_decision.rationale: Perfectly matches the learner's `conceptual_intuition` and interview-prep goal: they computed `n^(log_2 4) = n^2`, explained why the per-level work grows geometrically by a factor of 2 toward the leaves, and stated `Theta(n^2)`.

user_profile.what_user_wants_to_learn: Why solving normal equations (A^T A)x = A^T b directly squares the condition number compared to QR or SVD least squares.

module_context.module_title: Condition Numbers and Least Squares Stability
module_context.learning_objective: Prove that kappa_2(A^T A) = (kappa_2(A))^2 using singular values and explain its impact on floating-point precision.

prior_misconceptions: Confusing the determinant det(A) with the 2-norm condition number kappa_2(A) = sigma_max(A) / sigma_min(A)

question.prompt: Let A in R^(m x n) (m >= n) have full column rank with singular values sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= ... >= sigma_n > 0 and 2-norm condition number kappa_2(A) = sigma_1 / sigma_n. Using the SVD A = U Sigma V^T, prove that kappa_2(A^T A) = (kappa_2(A))^2, and state what happens in double-precision floating point (machine epsilon approx 10^(-16)) when kappa_2(A) = 10^9.
question.reference_answer: Substituting A = U Sigma V^T gives A^T A = V Sigma^T U^T U Sigma V^T = V (Sigma^T Sigma) V^T. Since Sigma^T Sigma = diag(sigma_1^2, ..., sigma_n^2), the singular values (and eigenvalues) of the symmetric positive-definite matrix A^T A are sigma_1^2 >= ... >= sigma_n^2 > 0. Therefore, kappa_2(A^T A) = sigma_1^2 / sigma_n^2 = (sigma_1 / sigma_n)^2 = (kappa_2(A))^2. When kappa_2(A) = 10^9, kappa_2(A^T A) = 10^18 > 1 / eps_mach (approx 10^16), so forming A^T A loses all significant digits in the smallest singular value direction and can make A^T A numerically singular in IEEE-754 double precision.
required_concepts_for_user_goal: deriving A^T A = V (Sigma^T Sigma) V^T so eigenvalues/singular values of A^T A are sigma_i^2
concluding kappa_2(A^T A) = sigma_1^2 / sigma_n^2 = (kappa_2(A))^2
numerical catastrophe in IEEE-754 float64: kappa_2(A^T A) = 10^18 exceeds 1/eps_mach (~10^16), wiping out all significant digits
question.grading_rubric: Requires showing A^T A has singular values sigma_i^2 so kappa_2(A^T A) = (sigma_1 / sigma_n)^2, plus comparing 10^18 against machine epsilon 10^(-16). Using determinants instead of singular values is incorrect.

user_submission.answer: Because det(A^T A) = det(A^T) * det(A) = (det(A))^2, the condition number squares. Since 10^9 is bigger than 0, the determinant is still positive so Gaussian elimination works fine without losing accuracy.

missed_concepts: deriving A^T A = V (Sigma^T Sigma) V^T so eigenvalues/singular values of A^T A are sigma_i^2
numerical catastrophe in IEEE-754 float64: kappa_2(A^T A) = 10^18 exceeds 1/eps_mach (~10^16), wiping out all significant digits
expected_decision.detected_misconception: Conflating the determinant det(A) (which isn't even defined for rectangular m x n matrices with m > n) with the spectral condition number kappa_2(A) = sigma_1 / sigma_n, and ignoring finite-precision rounding error when kappa_2(A^T A) = 10^18 > 1/eps_mach
expected_decision.feedback_focus: Clarify that (1) det(A) is undefined for non-square m x n matrices and does not measure conditioning, (2) A^T A = V diag(sigma_i^2) V^T squares the singular values so kappa_2(A^T A) = (sigma_1/sigma_n)^2 = 10^18, and (3) since 10^18 > 10^16 (1/eps_mach in float64), forming A^T A obliterates the smaller singular value information.
expected_decision.rationale: On attempt 2 with low recent accuracy (0.4), the learner repeated their misconception conflating determinants with singular-value condition numbers and missed the float64 precision loss completely. The Clef model marks `incorrect` and steps down to `ask_remedial_multiple_choice` to isolate the SVD identity `A^T A = V Sigma^T Sigma V^T`.
